newsitem.title: FRANCE: Toubon vows France will not bury sleaze probes.
newsitem.headline: Toubon vows France will not bury sleaze probes.

text.p: French Justice Minister Jacques Toubon gave an assurance on Wednesday that President Jacques Chirac's reform of the justice system would not be an excuse to bury political sleaze investigations.

However the investigative weekly which has exposed alleged illicit funding by Chirac's Gaullist RPR party said the Justice Ministry was again using procedural devices to slow probes into public works tenders in Paris while Chirac was mayor.
"If we want, as some people say, to turn the page on scandals, there is only one way to do that, which is for justice to be done," Toubon told Europe 1 radio.
"If there are offences that merit prosecution, there will be prosecutions. Justice must be done. We need good laws and an uncontested, serene judiciary," he said.
The minister added that Chirac's call for better protection of the presumption of innocence did not mean muzzling the press.

Politicians in the centre-right coalition have accused the media of violating the right of suspects to be presumed innocent by publishing evidence from investigations into party funding and corruption cases involving the ruling parties.

Dozens of businessmen and some key fundraisers have been placed under investigation on suspicion of having run a system of kickbacks on housing and public works contracts in the Paris region to fund the RPR. None has yet been brought to trial.

Le Canard Enchaine, the investigative and satirical weekly which has played a major role in exposing the funding networks, reported on Wednesday that the public prosecutor, after consulting Toubon's office, was set to reject an investigating magistrate's request for permission to extend his probe into more allegedly rigged public works tenders in Paris.
Under French law, if a magistrate discovers evidence of wrongdoing beyond the original offence he is probing, he must ask the prosecutor's office for authorisation to investigate it.

Le Canard Enchaine said magistrate Philippe Vandingenen, who is based in the Paris suburb of Creteil, would be ordered to hand over the case to the Paris public prosecutor because it fell outside his geographical area of responsibility.
The tactic has been used in the past to close investigations which suburban magistrates wanted to pursue.
